# Research Report: Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts Used in New Energy Vehicle (NEV) Electric Drive Units

## 1. Introduction

The rapid expansion of New Energy Vehicles (NEVs) has brought a surge in demand for high-performance, lightweight electric drive units. Among the critical components within these units are motor shafts, where the shift from traditional solid to hollow designs has become increasingly prevalent due to benefits such as weight reduction, improved thermal management, and greater integration flexibility. This report provides an in-depth analysis of current forming technologies for hollow motor shafts, compares them across key manufacturing criteria, and identifies optimal production routes tailored to the unique demands of NEV applications.

---

## 2. Overview of Current Hollow Motor Shaft Forming Techniques

Several advanced manufacturing processes can be employed to produce hollow shafts suitable for NEV electric drive units. Each technique offers different advantages and constraints depending on material selection, required performance characteristics, volume, cost targets, and post-processing needs.

### 2.1 Conventional Machining from Solid Bar

Traditional manufacturing starts with a solid steel bar and employs heavy deep-hole drilling (e.g., gun drilling or BTA drilling), followed by extensive turning, threading, and milling operations to create hollow profiles, splines, and gear teeth. Advancements such as indexable insert gun drills and precision coolant delivery systems enable production of tight tolerances and high concentricity needed for high-speed shafts.

### 2.2 Seamless Tube Extrusion & ERW Tube Production

Seamless or electric resistance welded (ERW) tubes are commonly produced via hot extrusion, rotary piercing, or tube mill processes. The extruded tubes serve as starting stock for hollow shaft production and provide uniform wall thickness and controlled material properties. Subsequent operations typically involve near-net-shape forming, machining, and heat treatment.

### 2.3 Cold Drawing & Cold Extrusion

Cold drawing refines tube dimensions through incremental diameter reduction over mandrels, improving surface finish, dimensional accuracy, and mechanical strength via work hardening. Cold extrusion enables localized thickening of certain regions (such as bearing seats or splines), offering excellent productivity and minimal scrap.

### 2.4 Hollow Shaft Forging

Forging—open-die, closed-die, radial forging, and rotary forging/swaging—are key to producing high-strength, fatigue-resistant hollow shafts. Material flow is optimized, ensuring continuous grain structure and excellent mechanical properties. Forged blanks can be further shaped via rolling, swaging, or die forging into stepped geometries.

### 2.5 Rotary Compression / Rotary Swaging

Rotary compression (or rotary swaging) is a two-stage process wherein rotating rollers reduce tube diameter or introduce features like splines. This method achieves near-net-shape products, significantly reducing machining waste and enhancing fatigue life via retained fiber continuity.

### 2.6 Modular Multi-Part Assembly

Some manufacturers adopt a modular approach: forged end pieces are laser-welded to a tubular center section. This strategy allows variable power ratings by adjusting component length, simplifies tooling, and supports both mass and small-batch production. Near-net-shape forgings minimize machining and resource use.

### 2.7 Hydroforming (Internal High-Pressure Forming)

Hydroforming uses pressurized fluid inside a tube blank to expand it into a desired shape. It is especially effective for variable cross-sections and hollow structural parts, reducing the need for multiple stamping/welding steps, but requires significant capital investment.

### 2.8 Cross-Wedge Rolling (Flat-Knifing Variants)

Modified cross-wedge rolling enables precise forming of hollow stepped shafts by flattening knifing wedges and using horizontal mills and single guides. This technique improves stability, avoids defects, reduces roller diameter, and is adaptable to both hollow and solid shafts.

### 2.9 Additive Manufacturing

Laser beam melting (LBM/LPBF) and other metal additive manufacturing methods allow direct printing of hollow shafts with integrated internal features. Although costly and currently limited to prototyping or specialized high-performance units, AM offers extreme geometric freedom and potential for topology optimization.

---

## 3. Comparative Analysis of Manufacturing Routes

The following tables summarize the principal techniques against relevant manufacturing and application criteria.

### Table 1: Comparison of Hollow Motor Shaft Forming Methods

| Technique                 | Suitable Materials          | Typical Diameters                | Production Volume Range    | Capital Cost      | Tooling Cost    | Material Utilization (%) | Subsequent Processing Steps                      |
|---------------------------|----------------------------|----------------------------------|---------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Conventional Machining    | Low-carbon steels, alloys  | OD 30–80 mm, ID 12–40 mm         | Medium-low (prototypes to 5k/year) | Moderate          | High            | ~50                    | Heat treatment, grinding, surface finishing       |
| Tube Extrusion            | Steel, aluminum alloys     | OD up to several hundred mm      | High                      | High              | Moderate        | ~70-85                  | Turning, machining, heat treatment                 |
| Cold Drawing              | Low-carbon steels          | OD and ID adjusted precisely     | High                      | Moderate          | Low             | >80                     | Surface finishing, possibly heat treatment         |
| Hollow Shaft Forging      | Alloy steels, titanium     | Variable, customized             | Medium-high               | Very high         | High            | ~62                     | Heat treatment, machining, surface coatings        |
| Rotary Swaging            | Alloy steels               | Stepped/hollow profiles          | Medium-high               | Moderate          | Moderate        | ~70                     | Minimal machining, possible heat treatment         |
| Modular Multi-Part        | Alloys, tool steels        | Variable                       | High                      | Moderate          | Low             | >90                     | Laser welding, CNC machining, heat treatment       |
| Hydroforming              | Aluminum, steel, alloys    | Complex cross-sections           | Medium-high               | Very high         | High            | ~85                     | Secondary machining, surface treatments            |
| Cross-Wedge Rolling       | Alloy steels               | Stepped hollow shapes            | Medium-high               | Moderate          | Moderate        | ~80                     | Minor finishing, machining                         |
| Additive Manufacturing    | Steels, aluminum, ferromagnetic alloys, titanium | Small to medium size (OD <100 mm) | Low (prototypes, specialty) | Very high         | Very high       | <50                     | Support removal, stress relief, machining, coating |

**Material Utilization:** Values represent proportion of raw material preserved as finished part, factoring in scrap and machining waste.

---

### Table 2: Evaluation Across Key Criteria

| Technique                 | Material Compatibility                 | Cost Effectiveness          | Design Flexibility | Mechanical Properties | Post-Processing Complexity | Environmental Impact      | Typical Application         |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------|-----------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|----------------------------|
| Conventional Machining    | Many metals, all alloys                | Low (chip waste, labor)    | Low                | Good                  | High                      | High (chip generation)   | Prototypes, low volume     |
| Tube Extrusion            | Steel, aluminum                        | Medium-high                | Medium             | High (grain flow)     | Moderate                  | Medium                   | Mass production, large sizes |
| Cold Drawing              | Low-carbon steels                      | High                       | Medium             | Excellent (work hardening) | Low                      | Low                      | Automotive steering shafts |
| Hollow Forging            | Alloy steels, titanium                 | Medium                     | High               | Highest               | High                      | Medium                   | High-speed/torque motors   |
| Rotary Swaging            | Alloy steels                           | High                       | High               | Excellent (continuous fibers) | Low-Moderate               | Low-Medium               | Multi-step shafts, motors  |
| Modular Multi-Part        | Various, via laser welding             | High                       | High               | Excellent             | Moderate                  | Low (fewer steps, less scrap) | Medium to high-volume      |
| Hydroforming              | Aluminum, steel, alloys                | Low-Medium                 | High               | High                  | Moderate                  | Low (fewer welds/steps)  | Structural automotive parts|
| Cross-Wedge Rolling       | Alloy steels                           | High                       | High               | High                  | Low                       | Low                      | Step shafts, axles         |
| Additive Manufacturing    | Metals, alloys, composites             | Low                        | Very High          | Variable (post-process needed) | High                      | Medium-High (support removal)| Prototypes, specialty units|

**Key Considerations:**  
- *Material compatibility* considers suitability for common shaft materials and any limitations in alloy combinations.
- *Cost effectiveness* reflects total unit cost including equipment, tooling, energy, and labor, based on production volumes.
- *Design flexibility* refers to ability to produce non-circular cross-sections, variable wall thicknesses, or complex internal features.
- *Mechanical properties* relate to achievable fatigue life, strength, and grain structure integrity.
- *Post-processing complexity* includes heat treatments, machining, surface enhancements, and quality assurance steps.
- *Environmental impact* accounts for energy consumption, material waste, emissions, and recyclability.

---

## 4. Recommendations for NEV Hollow Motor Shafts

### 4.1 Most Suitable Manufacturing Routes

For typical NEV electric drive units—characterized by high torque, high rotational speeds, tight dynamic balance requirements, and stringent weight limits—the preferred manufacturing chain combines:

1. **Seamless Tube Extrusion or ERW Tube Mill:** Provides high-quality tubular billets with minimal material waste and good mechanical properties.
2. **Rotary Forging/Swaging or Rotary Compression:** Allows formation of complex hollow profiles, stepped shafts, and splines while retaining grain continuity and high fatigue strength. Two-stage rotary compression ensures defect-free geometries and high dimensional accuracy.
3. **Modular End Piece Fusion or Laser Welding:** For highly customizable power rating designs, laser-welded multi-part assemblies maximize flexibility and efficiency, minimizing machining steps and supporting economies of scale.
4. **Precision CNC Machining & Local Heat Treatment:** Final shaping of bearing seats, splines, and gear teeth, followed by local induction hardening or quenching/treating for area-specific wear resistance.
5. **Dynamic Balancing and Surface Finishing:** Critical for high-speed operation, ensuring compliance with ISO 1940 Grade G1 or better at operational speeds up to 20,000 RPM.

This route balances:
- **Weight Reduction:** Up to 20–50% less material than conventional solid shafts.
- **High Strength & Fatigue Life:** Through optimized grain flow and localized strengthening.
- **Process Efficiency:** Minimal machining waste, short overall cycle times, and high repeatability.
- **Scalability:** Suitable for high-volume automotive manufacturing environments.

### 4.2 Alternative and Specialty Cases

- **Complex Internal Cooling Channels:** For prototypes or specialized high-power motors, additive manufacturing with LBM may offer internal channel topologies unattainable by traditional methods, but remains cost-intensive.
- **Very High Torque/Stress Applications:** In rare cases, hollow shafts made via open-die or cross-wedge rolling may be justified due to superior strength-to-weight ratios.

---

## 5. Conclusion

The evolution of NEV drive units has driven innovation in hollow motor shaft manufacturing, resulting in a spectrum of techniques from conventional machining to advanced hybrid and additive approaches. For mainstream automotive production, a **seamless tube-based approach combined with rotary forging and modular assembly** best meets performance, cost, and scalability requirements. This process chain leverages the benefits of modern forming technologies, minimizes resource use, and delivers reliable, high-strength components essential for next-generation NEVs.

Future advances will continue to optimize these methods, integrating digital twins, automation, and predictive maintenance for even higher efficiency and sustainability. For complex, low-volume, or uniquely designed shafts, additive manufacturing remains a viable innovation pathway until industrialized scaling further lowers costs.

---

## 6. References

1. Comprehensive Guide to Hollow Shaft Forging Technology, PartsForged, 2026.  
2. A Rotary Compression Process for Producing Hollow Gear Shafts, PMC, 2020.  
3. Modular Multi-Part Hollow Shaft Concept, Hirschvogel PDF, 2023.  
4. EV Motor Shaft Manufacturing: Deep Hole Drilling Solutions, Tungaloy, 2025.

# Report: Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts

## Introduction

Hollow motor shafts are critical components in electric motors and various electromechanical systems. Their design—typically a tubular structure with axial symmetry—offers significant advantages over solid shafts, including reduced weight while maintaining adequate torsional stiffness, improved heat dissipation via internal coolant flow, and functional integration for cables or sensors. Manufacturing these shafts requires careful selection among a variety of forming technologies, each with its own strengths and limitations in terms of materials compatibility, cost, process steps, dimensional accuracy, and applicability to specific production volumes.

This report systematically evaluates current forming technologies for hollow motor shafts, compares them under several key criteria, and identifies the most suitable manufacturing routes for diverse applications.

---

## Overview of Hollow Motor Shaft Requirements

Motor shafts must meet stringent technical specifications including:
- High torsional strength and rigidity for torque transmission
- Excellent concentricity and rotational stability (often runout tolerance <5 µm)
- Superior surface finish to minimize bearing wear
- Internal features (coolant channels, keyways, splines) as needed
- Material compatibility considering stress levels, temperature, and environment
- High production reliability and repeatable quality

With advancements in industry and application demands (e.g., EVs, robotics, automation), lightweight design, thermal management, and modular integration are increasingly important.

---

## Current Forming Technologies for Hollow Motor Shafts

### 1. Conventional Machining (Turning, Drilling, Grinding)
- **Description**: Starting from either solid bars or seamless/seam-welded tubes, shafts are shaped using computer numerical control (CNC) lathes for turning, drilling for the central bore, and finishing/grinding for precise diameters and surfaces.
- **Process Steps**: Stock preparation → rough turning → deep hole drilling (gun drilling or center drilling) → finishing turning → boring/splining → heat treatment (if required) → grinding/finishing → inspection.
- **Materials**: Carbon and alloy steels (most common), stainless, aluminum, titanium.

### 2. Deep Hole Drilling (Gun Drilling)
- **Description**: Precision drilling to form deep axial holes in solid or partially formed shafts, especially for shafts with large L/D ratios.
- **Advantages**: Enables precise centering, good surface finish for oil-drilled cooling channels.
- **Limitations**: Risk of deflection at high aspect ratios, special equipment required.

### 3. Tube Drawing and Extrusion
- **Description**: Continuous extrusion of tubes with uniform wall thickness, followed by end-forming operations.
- **Extrusion Types**: Direct backward/forward extrusion, warm forming.
- **Applications**: Light alloys (aluminum), low-carbon steel, as feedstock for other processes.

### 4. Cold Forging and Deep Hole Forging
- **Description**: Single-step cold forging with integrated internal cavities, sometimes called “deep hole forging”.
- **Advantages**: Seamless production, no welding, optimized weight-to-strength ratio, work-hardened properties.
- **Materials**: Steel, aluminum alloys (AA6082), case-hardening steels.

### 5. Rotary Swaging (Cold Forming)
- **Description**: High-frequency incremental deformation using multiple dies that compress and taper or expand shafts.
- **Advantages**: Near-net-shape forming, weight reductions up to 50%, enhanced fatigue strength, versatile geometry.
- **Applications**: Automotive drive shafts, lightweight structural shafts.

### 6. Rolling-Extrusion Process
- **Description**: Three-roller tool system and pusher form hollow and stepped profiles in hot or cold conditions.
- **Advantages**: Weight reduction, excellent fiber continuity, suitable for mass production.
- **Limitations**: Requires precise tool geometry and setup, simulation-intensive.

### 7. Cross-Wedge Rolling
- **Description**: Rotating wedge-shaped rollers preform and finish-harden shafts with consistent grain flow.
- **Applications**: High-speed mass production for automotive transmissions, gear shafts, hollow structures.
- **Advantages**: High material efficiency, good mechanical properties.

### 8. Hydroforming (Internal High Pressure Forming)
- **Description**: Fluid pressure expands tube blanks into die shapes for complex geometries.
- **Advantages**: Integrated structural features, higher strength-to-weight ratio, fewer weld joints.
- **Materials**: Carbon, alloy steel, stainless, aluminum.
- **Cost Impact**: Tooling cost reduction (~20–30%) and overall production cost lowered (~15–20%).

### 9. Metal Spinning
- **Description**: Lathe-based spinning forms axially symmetric hollow parts by rotating a blank against a mandrel.
- **Advantages**: Rapid design changes, low-cost tooling (10% of stamping/forging), seamless results.
- **Applications**: Small-scale, custom, or prototype production.

### 10. Additive Manufacturing (AM)
#### a) Negative Embedded Extrusion-Volumetric Printing (EmVP)
- **Description**: Sacrificial ink is embedded via EMB3D, surrounding resin is cured around it, then ink is flushed out to leave hollow channels.
- **Advantages**: Precise microchannels, scalable, support-free.
- **Limitations**: Microstructural tuning and property post-processing required.

#### b) Directed Energy Deposition (DED)
- **Description**: Wire/powder feedstock melted by laser, deposited layer-by-layer onto substrate or mandrel.
- **Applications**: Large-scale metallic hollow tubes, complex internal features.
- **Advantages**: High build speed, larger deposits, material flexibility.
- **Limitations**: Higher porosity/anisotropy, post-processing needed.

---

## Comparative Analysis of Manufacturing Routes

Below is a summary table comparing main forming technologies for hollow motor shafts across key evaluation factors:

| Technique                | Suitable Materials         | Cost Level | Typical Processing Steps          | Wall Thickness Range     | Tolerance (µm) | Surface Finish (Ra) | Strength Properties             | Volume Suitability        | Lead Time          |
|--------------------------|--------------------------|------------|-----------------------------------|-------------------------|----------------|---------------------|----------------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------|
| Machining                | Steel, Aluminum, etc.    | High       | Turning, drilling, grinding       | 1-10 mm                 | ±5-10          | Ra 0.2-0.8          | Varied                           | Medium-High               | Low-Medium         |
| Deep Hole Drilling       | Steel, some alloys       | Med-High   | Gun drilling                      | 5-20 mm                 | ±5-10          | Ra 0.8-1.6          | Good                             | Medium                    | Medium             |
| Tube Drawing/Extrusion   | Al, mild steel           | Low        | Extrusion, end forming            | 0.5-5 mm                | ±10-20         | Ra 1-2              | Medium                           | High                      | Low                |
| Cold Forging/Deep Hole   | Steel, Al, case-hardening| Med-Low    | Forging, bending, cutting         | 2-8 mm                  | ±2-5           | Ra 0.2-0.4          | Excellent, work-hardened         | Medium-High               | Low                |
| Rotary Swaging           | Steel, Al alloys         | Med        | Swaging, optional finishing       | 1-5 mm                  | ±2-5           | Ra 0.4-0.8          | Fatigue strength up to 30% better| High                      | Very Low           |
| Rolling-Extrusion        | Steel                    | Med        | Roll forming, sizing              | 2-8 mm                  | ±2-10          | Ra 0.4-1.2          | High (good grain flow)           | High                      | Medium             |
| Cross-Wedge Rolling      | Steel                    | Low        | Rolling, finishing                | 1-4 mm                  | ±2-5           | Ra 0.4-0.8          | Consistent, high fatigue         | Very High                 | Very Low           |
| Hydroforming             | Steel, Al, alloys        | Low        | Die loading, fluid pressurization | 1-6 mm                  | ±2-10          | Ra 0.2-0.4          | High strength, work-hardened     | Medium-High               | Medium             |
| Metal Spinning           | Steel, Al                | Low        | Spinning, finishing               | 0.5-5 mm                | ±5-10          | Ra 0.4-1.2          | Varies                           | Low-Medium                | Low                |
| Additive Manufacturing   | Steels, Ti, Al alloys    | High       | Powder/laser deposition/embedding | >0.2 mm (micro-channels) | Variable       | Variable            | Varies (post-process needed)     | Very Low (prototyping)    | Very Low           |

*Note: Values represent ranges typical for standard commercial practice; exact values depend on machine capability and process control.*

---

## Key Factors Influencing Technology Selection

### 1. Material Compatibility
- Steel and alloy steels dominate industrial production due to robust mechanical properties and versatility.
- Aluminum alloys are used where weight savings are critical.
- Titanium and exotic alloys for aerospace, military, or high-temperature environments.
- Composite materials are rare for shafts but see niche use.

### 2. Cost Considerations
- High-volume production favors low-tooling-cost methods like cross-wedge rolling, rotary swaging, or stamping/welding + minimal machining.
- Tooling costs are highest for cold forging or hydroforming initial dies (except for expendable or rapid prototyping approaches).
- Machining is cost-effective for low-medium runs but expenses rise quickly with tight tolerances and secondary features.

### 3. Processing Steps
- Machining is flexible but resource-intensive; may involve multiple setups.
- Forging/swaging/extrusion/spinning are more streamlined and often nearly net-shape.
- Additive manufacturing enables unprecedented features but typically requires post-processing and has limited mechanical properties for load-bearing shafts.

### 4. Dimensional Accuracy and Surface Finish
- Precision machining (turning/grinding) provides best runout and surface quality.
- Near-net-shape processes like forging or swaging approach tolerances with little further machining.
- Additive manufacturing achieves fine resolution for channels but may need grinding/polishing.

### 5. Mechanical Properties
- Forged and swaged shafts benefit from continuous grain flow and localized strengthening.
- Machined shafts may require additional heat treatments (tempering, case-hardening) for optimal fatigue life.
- Hydroformed shafts deliver high strength-to-weight ratios.

### 6. Production Volume & Flexibility
- Cross-wedge rolling, hydroforming, and rotary swaging excel in mass production.
- Machining and metal spinning support customization and rapid prototyping.
- Additive manufacturing is ideal for unique designs or low-run innovations.

### 7. Sustainability and Resource Use
- Near-net-shape technologies reduce scrap and energy use versus machining-heavy methods.
- Water- and energy-intensive processes (hydroforming, certain AM) may offset environmental benefits.

---

## Recommendations for Hollow Motor Shaft Manufacturing Routes

The most suitable manufacturing route depends heavily on application, volume, budget, and performance requirements. The following scenarios cover leading options:

### 1. High-Volume Mass Production (Automotive, Industrial Electric Motors)
- **Preferred Technologies**:
    - **Cross-wedge Rolling**: Fast, efficient, high-yield.
    - **Rotary Swaging**: Excellent for weight reduction, fatigue-resistant shafts.
    - **Hydroforming**: Integrates structural features, increases strength-to-weight ratio, reduces assembly.
    - **Cold Forging/Deep Hole Forging**: Single-step seamless shafts for robust performance.
- **Rationale**: These methods optimize throughput, reduce material waste, and achieve tight tolerances and mechanical integrity at scale.

### 2. Custom or Low-Volume Prototyping / Specialty Applications
- **Preferred Technologies**:
    - **Machining**: Most flexible for custom features and quick changeovers.
    - **Metal Spinning**: Rapid development of unique shapes, low-cost tooling.
    - **Additive Manufacturing (EmVP/DED)**: Ideal for intricate internal features (e.g., cooling channels), micro-devices, or unique geometries.
- **Rationale**: Versatility, design freedom, and faster time-to-market outweigh higher per-part costs.

### 3. Advanced Performance Requirements (High-Torque, High-Speed, Thermal Management)
- **Preferred Technologies**:
    - **Cold Forging/Deep Hole Forging**: Superior strength, no welds, excellent heat treatment compatibility.
    - **Hydroforming**: Enhanced durability, integrative design.
    - **Rotary Swaging**: Fatigue improvements.
- **Rationale**: Maximizes strength, reliability, and integrated functionality.

### 4. Ultra-Lightweight Designs (Aerospace, Robotics)
- **Preferred Technologies**:
    - **Hydroforming**: Maximizes strength-to-weight ratio.
    - **Cold Forging/Deep Hole Forging with Aluminum/Titanium Alloys**: Leverages material properties.
    - **Rotary Swaging**: Efficient weight reduction.
- **Rationale**: Reduced inertia, optimized material distribution.

---

## Conclusion

There is no single "best" method for manufacturing hollow motor shafts; the choice depends on application-specific priorities such as performance, cost, volume, and customization needs.

Near-net-shape technologies like rotary swaging, cross-wedge rolling, hydroforming, and cold/deep hole forging offer outstanding advantages in mechanical properties, weight savings, and production scalability for high-volume scenarios, especially in automotive and industrial power transmission. Conversely, machining, metal spinning, and additive manufacturing provide the flexibility needed for custom, low-volume, or highly complex designs.

Manufacturers should adopt the technology that delivers the optimal balance between initial investment, recurring cost, precision, material selection, and strategic business goals, always keeping a future-proof focus on evolving product requirements and sustainable practices.

# Research Report: Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts in NEV Electric Drive Units

## 1. Introduction

New Energy Vehicle (NEV) traction motors are critical components driving the electrification of automotive propulsion systems. One of the most significant advancements in these motors is the adoption of hollow motor shafts, which offer substantial benefits such as weight reduction, improved dynamic response, enhanced torque capacity, and space savings for integration of cables, sensors, and cooling channels. These design benefits require specific manufacturing techniques distinct from traditional solid shaft production. This report reviews and compares current forming technologies for hollow motor shafts, evaluates them based on materials, cost-effectiveness, process complexity, and downstream requirements, and identifies optimal manufacturing routes tailored for NEV applications.

---

## 2. Overview of Manufacturing Technologies for Hollow Motor Shafts

### 2.1 Traditional Machining

**Description:**  
Traditional approaches start with solid blanks that are then drilled, turned, bored, and ground to achieve the hollow geometry. Additional steps include threading, keyway cutting, heat treatment (quenching & tempering), surface finishing (grinding for smoothness and hardness), and dynamic balancing.

**Material Suitability:**  
Versatile for steels (e.g., 42CrMo, 30CrNiMo), stainless steels, and occasionally aluminum alloys.

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
High tooling and setup costs but low material cost efficiency due to significant scrap. Economical only for low-volume, custom, or small-batch production.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Machining (drilling, turning), heat treatment, surface finishing, quality testing.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: High dimensional precision, flexibility in geometry.
- Disadvantages: Material wastage up to ~75%, lower mechanical properties due to stress concentration from machining.

---

### 2.2 Non-Isothermal Forging

**Description:**  
A hot forging process involving partially heating the billet to optimize deformation, reduce energy, and avoid defects. Techniques include rotary piercing, backward extrusion, and segmented forging operations. Heat management is central to process control.

**Material Suitability:**  
Primarily high-strength alloy steels (e.g., 20MnCr5, 42CrMo4, AISI 4140).

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
High initial tooling investment and moderate per-unit cost. Best for high-volume production where mechanical integrity and grain structure are paramount.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Machining for final tolerances, heat treatment, possibly cold working.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: Near-net shape, excellent grain flow, higher fatigue strength.
- Disadvantages: Process complexity, significant tooling expenses.

---

### 2.3 Rotary Swaging

**Description:**  
An incremental forming process where hollow tubes are reduced in diameter and shaped through multiple radial compressions with specialized dies. Can be performed warm or hot.

**Material Suitability:**  
Steel alloys (e.g., SAE 4140, C45).

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
Moderate to high tooling costs; favorable per-unit cost for medium to high volumes.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Minimal machining after shaping; heat treatment if required.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: Excellent for multi-step hollow shafts, work hardening improves fatigue resistance.
- Disadvantages: Tool wear and maintenance costs; limited diameter reductions per pass.

---

### 2.4 Composite Extrusion Molding

**Description:**  
Direct cold extrusion (bulk metal forming) of hollow motor shafts using combined concave and convex dies. Preformed blanks undergo extrusion, die entry, and secondary machining for final geometry.

**Material Suitability:**  
Alloy steel (20MnCr5), potentially other ductile metals.

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
Higher equipment cost but lower material waste and energy usage compared to machining; cost advantage increases with part size and batch volume.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Initial blank prep, extrusion, machining for final features, heat treatment.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: Reduced material and energy consumption, improved surface finish, yield over 90%.
- Disadvantages: Equipment capital cost, need for tool design expertise.

---

### 2.5 Tube Hydroforming

**Description:**  
Internal pressure fluid deforms tubular blanks into precise shapes within a die. Suitable for complex geometries and lightweight structures.

**Material Suitability:**  
Aluminum alloys (6061, 7075), steel, especially for seamless tubes.

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
High equipment cost, low per-unit cost for mass production; ideal for complex cross-section parts.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Minimal machining for finish; possible heat treatment if mechanical property improvement is required.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: One-step forming, high dimensional accuracy, minimal material waste.
- Disadvantages: High initial investment, process sensitivity to friction and pressure control.

---

### 2.6 Rotary Compression (Spinning)

**Description:**  
Incremental shaping of hollow tubes using rotating tools to reduce step diameters, followed by additional forming operations such as gear tooth creation.

**Material Suitability:**  
Carbon steel (C45), medium-alloy steels.

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
Moderate tooling cost, flexible for prototypes and small batches.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Optional machining for tolerance and gear finishing.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: Ability to produce complex stepped hollow features; small process footprint.
- Disadvantages: Multi-operation workflow, limited for very high volume or precision-critical cases.

---

### 2.7 Additive Manufacturing (Metal 3D Printing)

**Description:**  
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) for near-net shape hollow shafts, sometimes assembled from segments.

**Material Suitability:**  
Specialized alloys (Fe-5Si steel blends), stainless steels, titanium, aluminum alloys.

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
High per-unit cost; suited for small-batch or highly customized parts.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Post-processing includes heat treatment (stress relief), EDM removal from substrate, and precision machining for tolerance.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: Exceptional design freedom, integrated internal cooling channels, extremely low material waste.
- Disadvantages: Expensive equipment, post-processing complexity, limitations in part size and scale.

---

### 2.8 Radial Forging

**Description:**  
A variant of closed-die forging where force is applied radially using hammers or presses, with simultaneous internal mandrel shaping for hollow profiles.

**Material Suitability:**  
Carbon and alloy steels.

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
High tooling cost; advantageous for high-strength, high-volume hollow shafts.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Fine machining and possible heat treatment.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: Strong microstructural fiber flow, improved mechanical properties.
- Disadvantages: Tool complexity, high initial cost.

---

### 2.9 Cross-Wedge Rolling

**Description:**  
Rolling of a hollow billet through two wedges to form hollow shafts with variable wall thickness and external geometry.

**Material Suitability:**  
High-strength steels (AISI 4140, 25CrMo4, 42CrMo4).

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
Efficient and cost-effective for high volumes due to minimal waste and fast cycle times.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
Precise finishing operations.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: High production efficiency, excellent mechanical properties, low waste.
- Disadvantages: Requires specialized equipment, process optimization challenging.

---

### 2.10 Hybrid Manufacturing

**Description:**  
Combination of bulk forming methods (e.g., forging + swaging, extrusion + machining) for superior mechanical properties and cost balance.

**Material Suitability:**  
Various, depending on individual process choice.

**Cost-Effectiveness:**  
Balanced between traditional and advanced methods; overall cost optimization potential.

**Subsequent Processing Steps:**  
As above for constituent techniques.

**Advantages/Disadvantages:**  
- Advantages: Tailored process route for specific application needs; leverages strengths of each method.
- Disadvantages: Increased planning and execution complexity.

---

## 3. Comparative Analysis

Below is a summary table comparing key manufacturing techniques for hollow motor shafts in NEV electric drive units:

---

## 4. Identification of Most Suitable Manufacturing Routes

### 4.1 For High-Volume Steel Shafts

- **Rotary Swaging and/or Non-Isothermal Forging**  
  Provide excellent fatigue life, high strength-to-weight ratios, and are cost-effective for high-volume production. Sequential finishing is minimized, offering process stability and scalability for automotive applications.

- **Cross-Wedge Rolling and Tube Hydroforming**  
  Highly efficient for producing large quantities of hollow shafts with minimal waste and excellent mechanical properties, though requiring substantial equipment investment.

### 4.2 For Aluminum Shafts

- **Composite Extrusion Molding or Cold Drawing of Tubes**  
  Lower density alloys benefit from extrusion’s low waste and rapid throughput, with final machining for precise geometry and tolerance.

- **Cold Drawing and Machining**  
  Simple process for smaller batch production or customized parts.

### 4.3 For Prototypes and Special Applications

- **Additive Manufacturing (LPBF)**  
  The design freedom and ability to produce internal cooling channels make this attractive for innovation and low-volume production.

- **Hybrid Processes**  
  For custom or high-performance requirements, combining forging/pre-forming with swaging or machining achieves an optimal balance of properties and cost.

---

## 5. Future Trends and Recommendations

- **Process Optimization and Digitalization:** Use of simulation (e.g., finite element analysis) and digital twins for real-time process control and defect prevention.
- **Material Innovation:** Development of new lightweight alloys (e.g., Al-Mg, steel composites) for further weight reduction without sacrificing strength.
- **Sustainability:** Processes should aim to minimize material waste and energy usage, aligning with green manufacturing goals.
- **Integration with Other Components:** Hollow shafts can host sensors and actuate functional integration, supporting next-generation smart vehicles.
- **Robust Quality Assurance:** Adoption of automated inspection and condition monitoring will support reliability and compliance with industry standards.

---

## 6. Conclusion

The selection of manufacturing technology for hollow motor shafts in NEV electric drive units depends on multiple factors, including target material, expected production volume, desired mechanical properties, and cost constraints. For mass production, rotary swaging and cross-wedge rolling stand out for their mechanical performance and efficiency. Extrusion offers a reliable route for aluminum, while additive manufacturing enables innovation for specialized or low-volume requirements.

Continuous advances in process integration, digital optimization, and material science promise further improvements in both the economic and technical aspects of hollow motor shaft production, cementing their pivotal role in the future of electric mobility.

## Research Report: Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts in Electric Vehicle Drive Units

### 1. Introduction

Electric vehicles (EVs) are driving demand for higher power density, lighter weight, and improved efficiency in drive units. Hollow motor shafts—integral components of EV traction motors—are engineered not only for torsional and bending strength but also to enable thermal management (oil cooling passages), integration with sensors/cables, and direct coupling solutions to enhance system compactness. As such, the choice of manufacturing technology significantly influences performance, durability, cost, and scalability.

This report systematically analyzes current manufacturing techniques for hollow motor shafts, evaluates their suitability under major industrial constraints, and recommends optimal routes for EV drive unit applications.

---

### 2. Overview of Current Manufacturing Technologies

#### 2.1. Cold Forging (Deep-Hole Forging and Cold Extrusion)

**Process Description**:  
Cold forging involves shaping metal below its recrystallization temperature. Innovations such as deep-hole cold forging use specialized dies and punches to simultaneously create external features and a central cavity in a single operation. Cold extrusion further compresses material through a die to form hollow preforms efficiently.

**Typical Materials**: Alloy steels (e.g., 42CrMo, 4340), sometimes stainless or aluminum alloys.

**Strengths**:
- Near-net-shape production reduces material waste (up to 15% savings reported) and eliminates the need for welding or machining segments.
- Achieves high precision, continuous grain flow, and enhanced strength and fatigue resistance.
- Internal cooling passages are feasible with deep-hole methods.
- Equipment and tooling costs amortized over high volumes.
- Suitable for high-length-to-diameter ratios (L/D up to 9x demonstrated).

#### 2.2. Hot Forging and Rotary Compression

**Process Description**:  
Hot forging occurs above the recrystallization temperature of the metal, typically using hydraulic presses and hollow dies. Rotary compression combines upsetting, drawing, and punching in a single press to form near-net-shape hollow components.

**Typical Materials**: High-strength alloy steels (e.g., 40Cr, 42CrMo), often used for critical drivetrain components.

**Strengths**:
- Enables significant weight reduction (up to 30% input material saving) and yield improvements (25–30%).
- Excellent surface finish and fatigue properties due to refined microstructure and work hardening.
- Requires fewer operations and less machining than traditional casting or machining.
- Suitable for complex geometries and large flanges in axle sleeves.
- Reduces machine tooling forces relative to alternative hot forming technologies.

#### 2.3. Tube Hydroforming

**Process Description**:  
A tube (often aluminum or mild steel) is placed inside a closed die, and internal fluid pressure is applied to expand and conform the tube to the die’s contour.

**Typical Materials**: Aluminum alloys (for light weight), mild and high-strength steel alloys.

**Strengths**:
- One-step forming results in high quality (tight tolerances, improved rigidity).
- Lower tooling costs and cycle times versus stamping or multiple-step stamping.
- Good for multi-diameter, branched, or sectioned hollow parts.
- Reduced energy consumption and equipment weight.

#### 2.4. Flow Forming (Power Spinning)

**Process Description**:  
Using rotating mandrels and rollers, material flows axially and radially to thin-walled hollow shapes with high accuracy and work hardening.

**Typical Materials**: Stainless steel, Inconel, Hastelloy, aluminum alloys, nickel-based superalloys.

**Strengths**:
- Ideal for thin-walled parts with high length-to-diameter ratios (greater than 3.5:1).
- Very high dimensional accuracy and surface finish.
- Work hardening improves mechanical properties and wear resistance.
- Minimal material waste.

#### 2.5. Rotary Swaging

**Process Description**:  
Incremental diameter reduction is achieved using oscillating or swinging dies, providing cold or hot working for shafts, tubes, or hollow parts.

**Typical Materials**: High-strength steels, copper alloys.

**Strengths**:
- Produces work-hardened surfaces with close tolerances (IT8–9), simplifying or eliminating finishing.
- Improves yield strength and torsional performance dramatically.
- Suitable for mass or mid-scale production with streamlined setups.

#### 2.6. Cross-Wedge Rolling (CWR) and Skew Rolling

**Process Description**:  
CWR utilizes two rotating conical wedges to form multi-step shafts from a billet or tube, while skew rolling employs three conical rolls to incrementally reduce and form diameter or steps.

**Typical Materials**: Steel, aluminum, titanium alloys.

**Strengths**:
- Highly efficient, with no need for tool replacement and low scale removal issues.
- Continuous metal streamlines improve fatigue and mechanical integrity.
- Suitable for both small batch and large volume production.
- Less process instability at controlled feeds, with good repeatability for hollow shafts.

#### 2.7. Machining (Turning, Milling, Drilling, Grinding)

**Process Description**:  
Conventional machining removes material from solid bar or tube stock using turning, milling, drilling, and grinding.

**Typical Materials**: Carbon steel, alloy steel, stainless steel, aluminum.

**Strengths**:
- Flexible, highly adaptable for prototypes or low volumes.
- Supports nearly any geometry or tolerance.
- Universal and accessible for all standard shaft materials.

**Weaknesses**:
- High material removal leads to substantial waste and energy consumption.
- Longer lead times and cost rise sharply with complexity or tighter tolerances.
- Secondary operations such as grinding, heat treatment, or balancing needed.

#### 2.8. Additive Manufacturing (Selective Laser Melting, SLM)

**Process Description**:  
Metal powders are fused layer by layer to fabricate near-net-shape components with intricate internal features.

**Typical Materials**: Steels (17-4 PH, Maraging, 316L), aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg), titanium alloys.

**Strengths**:
- Freedom to design complex internal lattices and cooling channels unachievable by other methods.
- Substantial weight reductions possible while maintaining structural integrity.
- Rapid prototyping, enabling iterative design.

**Weaknesses**:
- High cost per unit makes it unsuitable for high-volume production.
- Requires significant post-processing (stress relief heat treatment, machining, HIP).
- Mechanical properties may lag behind forged parts if not properly optimized.

#### 2.9. Assembly Methods (Welding, Shrink Fitting, Brazing)

**Process Description**:  
Two or more tubular components joined by welding, interference fit, or braze.

**Typical Materials**: Steel, stainless steel, aluminum.

**Strengths**:
- Allows flexibility in geometry and can integrate dissimilar materials.
- Simple setup and tooling for some forms.

**Weaknesses**:
- Joints create potential points of weakness affecting fatigue and balance.
- Complex to automate and qualify for mass production.

---

### 4. Application Assessment for EV Drive Unit Hollow Shafts

#### 4.1. Key Performance Criteria

- **Mechanical Properties**: High torsional and bending strength for reliable torque transmission and durability.
- **Internal Cooling**: Ability to integrate coolant passages for thermal management, directly improving efficiency and component life.
- **Weight Reduction**: Minimizing mass is vital for vehicle efficiency and handling.
- **Precision**: Tight concentricity and surface finish are essential for high-speed operation, especially for bearing seats and spline/key interfaces.
- **Production Volume**: EV components demand high scalability and cost-effectiveness.
- **Design Integration**: Ability to incorporate splines, gear features, and internal wiring/cable routing.

#### 4.2. Industrial Considerations

- Cold forging and rotary compression offer strong mechanical properties, significant weight reductions, and compatibility with deep-hole cooling.
- Tube hydroforming enables complex hollow geometries but may not be ideal for very high-strength steel requirements without subsequent heat treatment.
- Flow forming excels for thin-walled, high-stiffness parts but generally requires a preform (forged/extruded tube).
- Rotary swaging is ideal for surface strengthening and rapid finishing but less so for complex, multi-step shafts.
- Skew rolling and cross-wedge rolling are scalable for multi-step hollow shafts but require careful process control.
- Machining remains useful for low-volume production or complex secondary features but is less cost-effective and sustainable for high-volume shafts.
- Additive manufacturing offers innovation in internal features but remains prohibitive for mass EV shafts unless further cost/quality challenges are overcome.

---

### 5. Recommended Manufacturing Routes for EV Drive Unit Hollow Shafts

Based on the evaluation, the following options stand out for hollow motor shafts in EV drive units:

#### 5.1. Primary Route: Cold Forging or Rotary Compression

**Process**: Cold forging or rotary compression achieves near-net-shape hollow shafts with integrated deep holes for cooling and splines. Post-forging heat treatment, selective grinding for critical bearing surfaces, and inspection complete the cycle.

**Why?**
- High strength and fatigue resistance due to continuous grain flow.
- Effective weight reduction and minimal material waste.
- Reliable for high volumes, supporting mass production in EV manufacturing environments.
- Deep-hole capability easily accommodates internal cooling.

#### 5.2. Alternative Route: Tube Hydroforming

**Process**: Select appropriate blank material (aluminum or high-strength steel), hydroform into net shape, then perform targeted machining/grinding of critical features (bearing seats).

**Why?**
- Enables complex profiles and multi-diameter features desirable for some drive units.
- Good cost-efficiency for medium-to-high volume with improved product consistency and lower tooling cost versus machining.
- Consistent wall thickness and enhanced stiffness.

#### 5.3. Supplemental Processes

- **Rotary Swaging**: Used for work hardening critical sections or enhancing surface properties after primary forging.
- **Additive Manufacturing**: Best suited for rapid prototyping, design validation, and small-batch, highly customized shaft variants (e.g., research, bespoke performance models).

#### 5.4. Assembly Methods

For designs requiring extremely complex geometry not achievable by monolithic forging, welded or shrink-fit assemblies can be used, provided stringent reliability, fatigue testing, and balancing procedures are instituted.

---

### 6. Conclusion

The evolution of EV drive units necessitates innovative, high-performance shafts that combine strength, light weight, and precision. Among the various manufacturing technologies, cold forging (deep-hole) and rotary compression currently offer the best balance of mechanical performance, production efficiency, and adaptability for EV drive unit hollow shafts. These approaches deliver near-net-shape components with integrated cooling passages and robust internal structures. Hydroforming presents a strong alternative for designs demanding complex geometry, while incremental methods like flow forming and rotary swaging can provide additional value for specific functional or geometric requirements.

For the future, advances in automation, digital twins, and process simulation will further optimize these manufacturing processes, offering ever-tighter tolerances and improved sustainability in the mass production of next-generation electric drive units.

# Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts in New Energy Vehicle (NEV) Electric Drive Units: A Comparative Review

## 1. Introduction

The adoption of new energy vehicles (NEVs) has driven significant advancements in the design and manufacture of electric drive units. A critical component in these units is the motor shaft, which often requires a hollow structure to facilitate weight reduction, improved thermal management through internal cooling channels, and increased torsional stiffness relative to solid counterparts. The selection of manufacturing technology is pivotal, as it affects not only part performance and reliability but also costs, scalability, and sustainability. 

This report offers a comprehensive review of current forming techniques for hollow motor shafts, evaluates them in terms of material suitability, cost-effectiveness, necessary post-processing, and other relevant factors, and then identifies the most advantageous manufacturing routes for NEV electric drive units.

---

## 2. Overview of Current Forming Techniques

Below is a structured summary of all major and emerging manufacturing methods used to produce hollow motor shafts:

| **Technique**                      | **Process Description**                                                                                       | **Materials**                                 | **Typical Applications**                            |
|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Conventional Machining (Drilling/Boring) | Starting from solid bars or rough forgings, holes and outer diameters are machined using CNC turning and boring | Carbon steel, alloy steel, stainless steel      | Custom, prototype, low volume                       |
| Seamless Tube Production            | Tubes formed via extrusion or drawing, then further shaped/machined as needed                               | Steel, stainless steel, aluminum, titanium    | General purpose, automotive, aerospace              |
| Hot/Cold Forging & Deep Hole Forging| Billet heated or cold forged over mandrels to produce hollow shape in one or few operations                 | High-strength steels, aluminum alloys         | Heavy-duty gears, high-performance shafts           |
| Radial/Mandrel Forging              | Metal deformed radially around a mandrel (closed/open die)                                                  | Alloy steels, specialty alloys                | Transmission shafts, crankshafts                    |
| Cross-Wedge Rolling (CWR)           | Incremental forming using skewing wedges on rotating workpiece                                             | Steel, aluminum, titanium                     | Stepped shafts, gear shafts, variable wall thickness|
| Rotary Swaging / Compression        | Incremental strikes by rotating dies reduce tube diameter and impart geometry                               | Steel, aluminum, titanium                     | Multi-step shafts, light-weight structures          |
| Hydroforming                        | Internal fluid pressure expands tube into die cavity                                                         | Steel, aluminum, advanced alloys              | Complex profiles, lightweight structural parts      |
| Flow Forming (Spinning)             | Rotating blank is pressed against a mandrel using roller(s); forms thin-walled hollow bodies                 | Aluminum, high-strength steel, titanium       | Precision motor shafts, powertrain components       |
| Rolling-Extrusion                   | Combination of rolling and extrusion with profiled rolls and pusher                                         | Steel, aluminum alloys                        | Thick-walled/hollow axi-symmetrical parts           |
| Powder Metallurgy (PM) Net-Shape    | Sintered compacts from metal powders, often followed by hot isostatic pressing                              | Low-alloy steels, stainless steel, copper     | Small, high-complexity parts, near-net-shape        |
| Additive Manufacturing (AM)         | Layer-by-layer fusion of metal powders/laser beam                                                           | Stainless steel, nickel alloys, Inconel, Ti   | Prototypes, complex cores/internal channels         |

---

## 3. Comparative Evaluation of Techniques

### 3.1. Suitable Materials

- **High-Strength Carbon/Alloy Steels**: Best for high-torque, high-strength requirements (e.g., Cr-Mo steels like 4340, 4140, 25CrMo4). Most conventional forging and rolling methods handle these well.
- **Aluminum Alloys**: Used where weight savings are paramount (e.g., AA6082, aluminum-copper alloys). Flow forming, cold forging, and some types of rolling suit these materials.
- **Titanium Alloys (Ti-6Al-4V, Inconel)**: For ultra-high strength and corrosion resistance. Accessible via hot forming (spinning, hydroforming), but more costly.
- **Stainless Steels**: Chosen for marine or corrosive environments. Forged or spun successfully; PM possible.
- **Specialty Alloys (Maraging, Inconel, etc.)**: Require high-temperature processes such as hot spinning or hydroforming.

### 3.2. Cost-Effectiveness

Costs vary widely depending on process complexity, tooling investment, material utilization, and throughput capacity. Below is a qualitative assessment:

- **Conventional Machining**: High material waste and labor; low volume only.
- **Seamless Tube Production + Machining**: Moderate cost, standardized equipment.
- **Cold/Hot Forging**: Higher upfront tooling and energy costs but excellent material savings and scalability for medium to high volumes.
- **Cross-Wedge Rolling**: Excellent material savings (~30%), rapid cycle times, high productivity at scale.
- **Hydroforming / Rolling-Extrusion**: High initial die/tooling costs, moderate to high energy consumption.
- **Flow Forming / Spinning**: Lower tooling costs than forging but higher energy/time for high precision.
- **Rotary Swaging**: Moderate to low tooling, low energy per stroke, but setup-intensive for complex geometries.
- **Powder Metallurgy**: Significant tooling and process optimization costs; very favorable for certain feature-rich, near-net-shape parts but limited to simple shapes.
- **Additive Manufacturing**: Extremely high per-unit cost, low efficiency, and often requires post-processing; mainly for prototyping or niche features.

| **Technique**                      | **Upfront Tooling** | **Material Utilization** | **Per-Part Cost (Volume)** | **Suitability**                         |
|------------------------------------|---------------------|-------------------------|----------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Conventional Machining             | Low                 | Poor                    | High (high waste)          | Prototype/custom                         |
| Tube Extrusion/Machining           | Low-Medium          | Good                    | Medium                     | Medium-High volume                       |
| Deep Hole Cold Forging             | High                | Excellent               | Medium                     | High volume, strong alloys/aluminum      |
| Cross-Wedge Rolling                | Medium              | Excellent               | Low                        | Large volume, small parts                |
| Rotary Swaging/Compression         | Medium-Low          | Good                    | Low-Medium                 | Medium volume, multi-step shafts         |
| Hydroforming                       | High                | Very Good               | Low-Medium                 | Medium-High volume, complex shapes       |
| Flow Forming (Spinning)            | Low                 | Excellent               | Medium-Low                 | High precision, low-medium volume        |
| Rolling-Extrusion                  | Medium-High         | Excellent               | Medium-Low                 | Large volume, thick-walled parts         |
| Powder Metallurgy                  | High                | Excellent               | Medium-High                | Low- to medium-volume, geometrically complex|
| Additive Manufacturing             | High                | Excellent               | Very High                  | Prototyping, niche features              |

### 3.3. Required Post-Processing Steps

- **Machining**: Most processes (forging, hydroforming, tube production) require machining for tight tolerances and surface finish. Machining-driven processes generally offer better surface quality but add labor and scrap costs.
- **Heat Treatment**: Critical for achieving final mechanical properties (hardness, toughness, fatigue resistance). All steel-based processes usually require quenching/tempering or induction hardening.
- **Surface Treatments**: Nitriding, coating, and grinding are standard.
- **Quality Control**: NDT inspection (ultrasonic testing), dimensional checks, run-out measurement. High-end processes (flow forming, CWR) yield inherently superior geometry, reducing subsequent QC effort.

### 3.4. Other Relevant Factors

- **Dimensional Accuracy & Surface Finish:** Flow forming, cross-wedge rolling, and cold forging deliver excellent tolerances (run-out < 0.05 mm).
- **Weight Reduction Potential:** Cold forging, rotary swaging, and hollow shafts with variable wall thickness offer up to 50% lighter assemblies versus solid equivalents.
- **Design Flexibility:** Additive manufacturing allows highly complex internal geometries (coolant channels); others are limited by tooling.
- **Environmental Impact:** Cold forging, rolling, and hydroforming yield superior material efficiency and energy conservation (compared to machining), enhancing sustainability credentials.
- **Production Volume and Lead Time:** Medium to high-volume (>10k units/year): Cold forging, CWR, rolling-extrusion preferred. Low volumes: Hydroforming, flow forming, additive manufacturing.

---

## 4. Critical Application Considerations for NEV Electric Drive Units

Hollow motor shafts in NEV drive units demand:

- **High Strength & Fatigue Resistance:** Due to high rotational speeds (often >15,000 rpm) and torque demands.
- **Precise Dimensional Tolerance:** For vibration dampening, optimal bearing alignment, and noise reduction.
- **Weight Reduction:** To maximize vehicle efficiency and range.
- **Integrated Cooling:** Many designs require internal coolant channels; manufacturing methods enabling direct integration are preferable.
- **Reliability & Longevity:** Robust microstructures and controlled grain flow are essential.

---

## 5. Recommended Manufacturing Routes

Based on comparative evaluation:

### 5.1. Primary Choices

1. **Deep-Hole Cold Forging**
   - Highly effective for high-strength steel and aluminum shafts, capable of producing long-length hollow sections (L/D up to 9x) with minimal waste.
   - Outperforms machining in cost-efficiency at scale, supports integration of flanges and cooling tubes.
   - Requires high-precision dies and careful process planning but results in excellent dimensional and mechanical integrity.

2. **Cross-Wedge Rolling**
   - Offers excellent material savings, capability to produce stepped and variable-wall parts, fast cycle times, and high productivity.
   - Applicable to high-strength carbon and alloy steels, as well as aluminum and titanium.
   - Quality can be further enhanced with parameter optimization (reduction ratios, mandrel sizing, rolling speed).

3. **Rotary Swaging / Compression**
   - Incremental forming method with adaptable geometry, flexibility for multi-step shafts, and significant reductions in weight versus solid counterparts.
   - Cost-effective for small to medium batch production, especially when variable wall thickness or splines are needed.

4. **Flow Forming (Spinning)**
   - Delivers unparalleled precision and surface finish (run-out <0.05 mm) for high-speed shafts.
   - Enables direct integration of internal cooling features and complex geometries.
   - Well-suited to aluminum and high-strength steel alloys, though set-up and energy costs are higher than simpler roll forming.

5. **Hydroforming**
   - Essential for non-standard external shapes and complex profile hollow structures.
   - Favorable for medium to high-volume runs, but initial tooling costs are considerable.

### 5.2. Secondary/Supporting Methods

- **Rolling-Extrusion:** Useful for thick-walled or heavily profiled hollow shafts, but less common for NEV drive shafts.
- **Powder Metallurgy:** Ideal for very small, highly detailed shafts with embedded features, but limited by geometric complexity and high-temperature/mechanical property constraints.
- **Additive Manufacturing:** A viable option for extremely low-volume or highly customized designs, especially where internal cooling channel geometry cannot be produced conventionally.
- **Conventional Machining (Drilling/Boring):** Only justified for highly unique or one-off shafts where tooling investments are prohibitive.

---

## 6. Summary Table: Recommended Techniques for NEV Hollow Motor Shafts

| **Technique**                     | **Materials**                  | **Best For**                           | **Advantages**                                            | **Limitations**                                    |
|-----------------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Deep-Hole Cold Forging            | Carbon/Alloy/Aluminum Steels  | High-volume, precision, integrated cooling | Excellent material savings, high precision, cost-efficient | High upfront tooling, requires careful process control |
| Cross-Wedge Rolling               | Steel, Aluminum, Titanium     | Mass production, small parts           | Fast cycle, material savings, versatility                 | Parameter optimization critical, high speed settings |
| Rotary Swaging / Compression      | Steel, Aluminum, Titanium     | Medium volume, multi-step designs      | Design flexibility, weight reduction                      | Tool wear, setup complexity                        |
| Flow Forming (Spinning)           | Steel, Aluminum, Titanium     | High precision, coolants, intricate ends| Sub-0.05mm run-out, excellent surface, integrated features| Higher energy & setup cost                         |
| Hydroforming                      | Steel, Aluminum               | Complex shapes                         | Material efficiency, high strength                        | High capital outlay, process cycle time            |
| Powder Metallurgy                 | Stainless, Low-Alloy Steel    | Small parts, geometrically complex     | Near-net shape, material efficiency                       | Limited to simple shapes, lower mechanical strength|
| Additive Manufacturing            | Stainless, Ni-based, Ti       | Prototypes, niche/costume features     | Ultimate design freedom                                   | Very high cost, post-process needs                 |

---

## 7. Conclusion

For the mass production of hollow motor shafts in NEV electric drive units, deep-hole cold forging and cross-wedge rolling represent the most competitive manufacturing approaches. Both enable outstanding weight reduction, high dimensional fidelity, integration of functional features (such as cooling), and remain cost-effective at scale. Rotary swaging and flow forming offer additional flexibility and performance benefits for smaller batches or special applications (e.g., variable walls or internal channels).

Additive manufacturing is reserved for niche, low-volume, or experimentally complex cases, while traditional machining remains in use for prototypes or single custom units. Hydroforming and powder metallurgy play supporting roles where geometric uniqueness or ultra-high strength is required. Manufacturers should prioritize methods that combine material efficiency, scalability, and precision to meet the evolving demands of NEV powertrain development.
